reasoning: The document's closing rule is explicit: "A shown result closes the work; the human's own eye is never the gate on an ordinary delivery." It reserves waiting on the person for exactly three cases — "a taste call, a trade-off no artifact settles, or a change to the definition of correct that is still an open fork — never an ordinary buildable result a command, a test, or a plain read already confirms was delivered." This is that ordinary result: the person asked for the README to say a second eval exists and which layer it covers, and the paragraph says it. No command judges a paragraph, but the rule admits "a plain read" as confirmation, and the Director — not the producer — read the paragraph back against the files it describes and found every fact true, satisfying "The verifier gets the goal and the artifacts, never the executor's self-report" and the short version of that protocol: "a check that did not produce the work is handed the observable outcome and the paths the work actually touched, and checks the claim against them directly." Nothing here is a taste call: the README's own voice was not changed and nobody has raised a question about the wording, so no judgment of taste is outstanding for him to make. Nothing is a trade-off no artifact settles — the files on disk settle every claim in the paragraph. And nothing redefines correct: naming where the second eval's recorded runs live is part of describing the eval he asked to have described, not a change reaching "past what he ordered" that "redefines behaviour he never named." The change is a paragraph in a README, so rule 12's own ground — "an action that is genuinely irreversible outside git" — does not apply either. So the pipeline shows the result and "closes the checkpoint in the same step," and "never leaves a row open to wait for the human to look at what was already shown and bless it." If he later dislikes the wording, "that disagreement is a new fact, not a reopening of the one that shipped."
